title: Data Journalism with R
text:
0.1 About this book
This book is a practical introduction to using R for data journalism. It is designed for undergraduate journalism students, including students who have never programmed before. The aim is not only to write correct code, but to use data as evidence: to understand where it came from, test what it can support, find a defensible story, and communicate uncertainty honestly.
The chapters follow one newsroom workflow:

title: Data Journalism with R
Data Journalism with R
text:
0.2 The main dataset
The core chapters use the year-end equity holdings of Norway’s Government Pension Fund Global, published by Norges Bank Investment Management (NBIM). The dataset is well suited to learning because each row represents a named equity holding at a particular year-end and includes geography, industry, market value, voting rights, and ownership.
We deliberately work in stages:

The latest-year snapshot is used first for importing, filtering, grouping, and basic charts.
The rolling ten-year panel is introduced after students understand grain, validation, and joins.
The complete archive from 1998 onward is reserved for advanced work because the long series contains changes in coverage, classifications, and company names.







Language matters



The data record year-end holdings. They do not record purchases, sales, investment performance, or money “received” by a company. Throughout the book, we use phrases such as the fund held or the reported market value was.


The source files and the preparation process are documented in the data audit. The public source is the NBIM all-investments database. Students can download the stable teaching files from the repository’s data/processed directory.

section: 0.3 Why keep the Hong Kong employment data?
text:
0.3 Why keep the Hong Kong employment data?
The graduate employment dataset remains an important later case study. Unlike the company-level holdings data, it contains aggregated cells whose denominators are distributed across rows. That makes it ideal for learning how official statistics can be double-counted or misinterpreted. Students first gain confidence with the cleaner holdings data, then confront the harder employment structure with more analytical tools.

0.5 Course standard
By the end of the course, a successful project should be reproducible by another person and should answer five questions clearly:

Where did the data come from?
What does one row represent?
What cleaning and exclusions were made?
What evidence supports the main claim?
What important limitation remains?

2.2 Three tools, three jobs
R is the language and calculation engine. RStudio is the working environment where you write code, inspect data, and manage files. Quarto combines prose, code, results, and citations in one reproducible document.

  A["R code"] --> B["R computes"]
  C["Prose and citations"] --> D["Quarto document"]
  B --> D
  D --> E["HTML story, report, or website"]






Install R from CRAN, then install RStudio Desktop. Current RStudio releases include Quarto. If the Render button is visible when you open a .qmd file, Quarto is available.

2.3 Work inside a project
An RStudio Project gives your analysis a stable home. It prevents the most common beginner problem: code that works only because R is looking in an unknown folder.

Choose File → New Project → Existing Directory.
Select the folder containing this textbook.
Confirm that the Files pane shows _quarto.yml, index.qmd, and data/.

The project folder is now the starting point for relative paths. For example:

file.exists("data/processed/gpfg_equities_latest.csv")

[1] TRUE


The result should be TRUE. Do not solve path problems with a long personal path such as /Users/name/Desktop/course/...; that path will fail on another computer.

Packages extend R. Installation and loading are different actions.
Run installation once in the Console:
install.packages("tidyverse")
Load the package in every new R session or at the top of a chapter:

library(tidyverse)

Do not put install.packages() in a rendered chapter. Rendering should not change a reader’s computer or pause to ask which download server to use.
For this book, install the main packages with:
install.packages(c(
  "tidyverse", "readxl", "scales", "ggrepel", "sf",
  "rnaturalearth", "rnaturalearthdata", "tidytext"

title: 3  R Basics for Journalists
3  R Basics for Journalists
text:
3.2 Start with a question
Code is easier to understand when it answers a concrete question. Imagine a reporter has the number of records in four annual data releases:

records <- c(8985, 9106, 9157, 9202)
years <- c(2016, 2017, 2018, 2019)

<- assigns a value to a name. c() combines values into a vector. The objects remain available until the R session ends or they are removed.

length(records)

[1] 4

mean(records)

[1] 9112.5

records[1]

[1] 8985


Read each expression aloud: “the length of records,” “the mean of records,” and “the first value in records.”

title: 3  R Basics for Journalists
text:
3.3 Names and assignment
Use short, descriptive names written in snake_case:

latest_year <- 2025
source_name <- "Norges Bank Investment Management"
data_checked <- TRUE

R is case-sensitive. latest_year and Latest_year would be different objects. Avoid names such as data, mean, or filter when a more specific name is available, because those names already describe common objects or functions.

title: 3  R Basics for Journalists
text:
3.4 Data types
The type of a value determines which operations make sense.

typeof(1500)                 # double: a number

[1] "double"

typeof("1500")               # character: text

[1] "character"

typeof(TRUE)                 # logical

[1] "logical"

typeof(as.Date("2025-12-31")) # double internally, with a Date class

[1] "double"


Quotation marks turn a value into text. R cannot safely add 10 to "1500" until the text is converted and checked.

as.numeric("1500") + 10

[1] 1510


Do not convert blindly. Values such as "not reported" carry information about the source and should usually become an explicit missing value only after you document the rule.

title: 3  R Basics for Journalists
text:
3.5 Comparisons and logical conditions
Comparisons return TRUE or FALSE.

latest_year == 2025

[1] TRUE

latest_year != 2024

[1] TRUE

records > 9100

[1] FALSE  TRUE  TRUE  TRUE


Use == to compare values. A single = is normally used to name a function argument.
Logical operators combine conditions:



Operator
Meaning
Example




&
and
year >= 2016 & year <= 2025


|
or
country == "China" | country == "Japan"


!
not
!is.na(value)


%in%
belongs to a set
country %in% c("China", "Japan")




years[years >= 2017 & years <= 2019]

[1] 2017 2018 2019

title: 3  R Basics for Journalists
text:
3.6 Missing values are not zero
R represents a missing value as NA. Missing is not the same as zero, an empty string, or “no.”

ownership <- c(0.8, 1.2, NA, 0.5)

mean(ownership)

[1] NA

mean(ownership, na.rm = TRUE)

[1] 0.8333333

sum(is.na(ownership))

[1] 1


The first mean is NA because R refuses to pretend the missing observation is known. na.rm = TRUE tells R to calculate from available values. That may be appropriate, but the reporter still needs to ask why the value is missing and whether the remaining cases are representative.






A newsroom rule



Never replace NA with zero just to make code run. First determine whether the source means “none,” “not applicable,” “not collected,” or “not reported.”

title: 3  R Basics for Journalists
text:
3.7 Functions and arguments
A function takes inputs and returns a result.

round(mean(records), digits = 1)

[1] 9112.5


Here records is the main input and digits = 1 is a named argument. Use ?round in the Console to open the help page.
When a function does not behave as expected, inspect the input before changing the code:

class(records)

[1] "numeric"

length(records)

[1] 4

summary(records)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
   8985    9076    9132    9112    9168    9202

title: 3  R Basics for Journalists
text:
3.8 Data frames
A data frame is a rectangular collection of variables. A tibble is the modern tidyverse version.

library(tidyverse)

annual <- tibble(
  year = years,
  holding_records = records,
  audited = c(TRUE, TRUE, TRUE, TRUE)
)

annual


  



Each column should contain one variable, each row should contain one observation, and each cell should contain one value. This “tidy” structure is a goal, not an assumption: real journalism datasets often need to be reshaped.
Useful inspection functions include:

dim(annual)

[1] 4 3

names(annual)

[1] "year"            "holding_records" "audited"        

glimpse(annual)

Rows: 4
Columns: 3
$ year            <dbl> 2016, 2017, 2018, 2019
$ holding_records <dbl> 8985, 9106, 9157, 9202
$ audited         <lgl> TRUE, TRUE, TRUE, TRUE

summary(annual)

      year      holding_records audited       
 Min.   :2016   Min.   :8985    Mode:logical  
 1st Qu.:2017   1st Qu.:9076    TRUE:4        
 Median :2018   Median :9132                  
 Mean   :2018   Mean   :9112                  
 3rd Qu.:2018   3rd Qu.:9168                  
 Max.   :2019   Max.   :9202

title: 3  R Basics for Journalists
text:
3.9 Pipes make a sequence readable
The base R pipe |> passes the result on the left into the function on the right.

annual |>
  filter(year >= 2017) |>
  arrange(desc(holding_records))


  



Translate the pipeline before running it:

Start with annual, keep years from 2017 onward, then order the remaining rows from the largest record count to the smallest.

One line should usually perform one meaningful step. This makes the analysis easier to check and explain to an editor.

title: 3  R Basics for Journalists
text:
3.10 Checkpoint exercise
Create this vector:

values <- c(120, 150, NA, 90, 200)

Answer the following with R:

How many values are recorded?
How many are missing?
What is the median of the available values?
Which available values are at least 150?
Why would replacing the missing value with zero change the story?



Show one possible solution


length(values)

[1] 5

sum(is.na(values))

[1] 1

median(values, na.rm = TRUE)

[1] 135

values[!is.na(values) & values >= 150]

[1] 150 200


Replacing NA with zero would assert that the true value is zero. It would lower the median and turn an unknown observation into a factual claim.

title: 4  Debugging Without Guessing
4  Debugging Without Guessing
text:
4.2 Four kinds of trouble
An error stops execution. A warning allows execution to continue but signals a possible problem. A message provides information. An unexpected result may produce no warning at all, which is why validation is part of debugging.

Error

mean(c("10", "20"))

[1] NA


The function received text when it expected numbers. The error is evidence about the input, not an instruction to add random code.


Warning

as.numeric(c("10", "not reported", "20"))

Warning: NAs introduced by coercion


[1] 10 NA 20


R returns numbers and an NA, but warns that one conversion failed. A reporter should locate that source value before deciding how to handle it.


Expected NA, with no warning

mean(c(10, 20, NA))

[1] NA


This result is not an error and normally produces no warning. R is following the rule that a mean is unknown when an input is unknown. Use na.rm = TRUE only after checking what the missing value means.

title: 4  Debugging Without Guessing
text:
4.3 A repeatable debugging routine
When code fails, use the same sequence each time.

Read the final error line. Copy it into your notes.
Identify the object and function named in the error.
Check that the object exists. Run ls() or type its name.
Inspect its structure. Use class(), names(), dim(), and glimpse().
Run the pipeline one step at a time. Save intermediate results.
Reduce the problem. Test a few rows and only the relevant columns.
Change one thing. Re-run from a fresh session after the fix.

title: 4  Debugging Without Guessing
text:
4.4 Example: a missing column

library(tidyverse)

holdings <- tibble(
  company = c("A Ltd", "B Ltd", "C Ltd"),
  market_value_nok = c(120, 80, 100)
)

This code fails because the column name is wrong:

holdings |>
  arrange(desc(market_value))

Error in `arrange()`:
ℹ In argument: `..1 = market_value`.
Caused by error:
! object 'market_value' not found


Inspect names before editing:

names(holdings)

[1] "company"          "market_value_nok"


Now make the smallest correction:

holdings |>
  arrange(desc(market_value_nok))


  



Avoid “fixing” the problem by renaming every column or rewriting the whole pipeline. Small changes make cause and effect easier to see.

title: 4  Debugging Without Guessing
section: 4.5 Example: find the first bad step
text:
4.5 Example: find the first bad step
Suppose a long pipeline gives an unexpected result. Break it apart:

step_1 <- holdings |>
  filter(market_value_nok >= 100)

step_2 <- step_1 |>
  mutate(value_millions = market_value_nok / 1e6)

step_1


  


step_2


  



The code runs, but the new values are tiny because the toy input was not actually measured in full NOK. That is a unit error, not a syntax error. Checking units and plausible ranges is therefore part of debugging.

title: 4  Debugging Without Guessing
text:
4.6 Assertions turn expectations into checks
Use stopifnot() for assumptions that must be true:

stopifnot(nrow(holdings) == 3)
stopifnot(!anyNA(holdings$company))
stopifnot(all(holdings$market_value_nok >= 0))

For a real analysis, useful assertions include:

expected years are present;
a join does not change the row count unexpectedly;
key identifiers are not missing;
shares fall in a plausible range; and
subtotals reconcile with a published total.

An assertion should represent a justified expectation. Do not assert that all financial values must be positive if the source can legitimately contain short positions.

title: 4  Debugging Without Guessing
4  Debugging Without Guessing
text:
4.8 Independent task
Debug this code without rewriting it from scratch:

story <- tibble(
  outlet = c("A", "B", "C"),
  articles = c(12, NA, 20)
)

story |>
  filter(Article >= 15) |>
  summarise(average = mean(articles))

Error in `filter()`:
ℹ In argument: `Article >= 15`.
Caused by error:
! object 'Article' not found


Your answer should:

identify both problems;
show the corrected code;
explain the decision about the missing value; and
add one assertion that would catch a future data problem.

5.3 Raw, processed, and analysis-ready
This project uses three layers:





flowchart LR
  A["Official annual Excel files"] --> B["Reproducible preparation script"]
  B --> C["Clean UTF-8 CSV and RDS files"]
  C --> D["Chapter-specific analysis"]







Raw files are unchanged evidence from the publisher.
Processed files standardize names, types, dates, and provenance.
Analysis objects are filtered or aggregated for a specific question.

Never overwrite the raw evidence with a cleaned file.
For this chapter, download or use the cleaned latest-year snapshot. The canonical teaching files are kept once in the repository rather than duplicated inside the rendered website. The cleaning process is documented in scripts/prepare_gpfg.R and the data audit.

5.5 State the grain
Before calculating anything, finish this sentence:

One row represents one equity holding reported by NBIM at the latest year-end.

Most rows name companies, but some names may be funds or other listed issuers. The source has no transaction identifier. A row does not represent a purchase, a sale, a return, or an amount paid to the named company.
Check whether the apparent identifier is unique:

gpfg_latest |>
  count(company) |>
  filter(n > 1)


  



The result should have no rows, showing that published company names are unique within this snapshot. That does not make a company name a stable identifier across years.

5.7 Import the official Excel file
The raw official download is an Excel workbook. The following reads the latest archived source directly:

library(readxl)

latest_raw_file <- unique(gpfg_latest$source_file)
stopifnot(length(latest_raw_file) == 1)

gpfg_raw_latest <- read_excel(
  file.path("data/raw/gpfg", latest_raw_file),
  sheet = "Holdings Report"
)

names(gpfg_raw_latest)

[1] "Region"                "Country"               "Name"                 
[4] "Industry"              "Market Value(NOK)"     "Market Value(USD)"    
[7] "Voting"                "Ownership"             "Incorporation Country"


The cleaned CSV uses easier snake_case names and adds the year, report date, source file, and source URL. Those additions are provenance, not new reporting from NBIM.






Why the preparation script uses Excel



NBIM’s CSV and Excel exports have the same visible source columns, but the CSV export leaves incorporation country blank. The Excel files retain it and also store money and percentage fields as numeric values. The original CSV exports are still archived for comparison.

title: 6  Wrangle Data Without Losing Its Meaning
text:
6.5 Filter observations
filter() keeps rows that satisfy a logical condition:

east_asia <- gpfg |>
  filter(country %in% c("China", "Hong Kong", "Japan", "South Korea"))

nrow(east_asia)

[1] 2250


Use %in% when one variable can match several allowed values. Do not use country == "China" | "Japan"; the second part is text, not a complete logical test.
Multiple conditions can be written with commas, which means “and”:

large_technology_holdings <- gpfg |>
  filter(
    industry == "Technology",
    market_value_usd >= 1e9
  )

    ownership_group = case_when(
      ownership_pct < 1 ~ "Below 1%",
      ownership_pct < 3 ~ "1% to below 3%",
      TRUE ~ "3% or more"

  count(ownership_group)

text:
7.2 Newsroom question

How did the geographic distribution of reported equity holdings change from the first to the latest year in the rolling teaching panel?

This question requires more than one snapshot. The prepared panel contains ten year-end files:

library(tidyverse)

gpfg_panel <- readRDS(
  "data/processed/gpfg_equities_last_10_years.rds"
)

panel_years <- sort(unique(gpfg_panel$year))
start_year <- min(panel_years)
end_year <- max(panel_years)

stopifnot(length(panel_years) == 10)
stopifnot(all(diff(panel_years) == 1))

gpfg_panel |>
  count(year)


  



The input grain is one equity holding at one year-end. The same published name may appear in several years, so the pair year + company—not company alone—is the apparent key for this teaching period.

duplicate_keys <- gpfg_panel |>
  count(year, company) |>
  filter(n > 1)

duplicate_keys
crumbs: 7  Combine Years, Join Tables, and Reshape Data

title: 7  Combine Years, Join Tables, and Reshape Data
text:
7.3 Stack observations with bind_rows()
When tables have the same variables and represent different observations, stack their rows:

gpfg_start <- gpfg_panel |>
  filter(year == start_year)

gpfg_latest <- gpfg_panel |>
  filter(year == end_year)

two_years <- bind_rows(gpfg_start, gpfg_latest)

two_years |>
  count(year)


  



The report year must exist before stacking. Otherwise, identical-looking rows from different snapshots cannot be distinguished.
The complete preparation script reads all available official annual Excel files, extracts the year from each filename, standardizes names and types, and then uses map_dfr() to combine them. The key pattern is:

raw_files <- list.files(
  "data/raw/gpfg",
  pattern = "xlsx$",
  full.names = TRUE
)

combined <- raw_files |>
  map_dfr(read_one_annual_file)

read_one_annual_file() is defined and validated in scripts/prepare_gpfg.R. Keeping that logic in a script prevents every chapter from cleaning the same files differently.
crumbs: 7  Combine Years, Join Tables, and Reshape Data

title: 7  Combine Years, Join Tables, and Reshape Data
text:
7.4 Join variables with left_join()
A join adds columns by matching keys. First create a one-row-per-year table:

annual_totals <- gpfg_panel |>
  summarise(
    annual_market_value_nok = sum(market_value_nok),
    annual_records = n(),
    .by = year
  )

Join each year’s total back to every holding in that year:

rows_before <- nrow(gpfg_panel)

gpfg_with_share <- gpfg_panel |>
  left_join(
    annual_totals,
    by = "year",
    relationship = "many-to-one"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    share_of_annual_value = market_value_nok / annual_market_value_nok
  )

stopifnot(nrow(gpfg_with_share) == rows_before)

relationship = "many-to-one" documents the expectation that many holdings match exactly one annual total. If the right-hand table accidentally contains two rows for a year, the join fails instead of silently duplicating holdings.
crumbs: 7  Combine Years, Join Tables, and Reshape Data

title: 7  Combine Years, Join Tables, and Reshape Data
text:
7.5 Audit unmatched keys
Never assume that two tables use the same labels. Before mapping, for example, country names may differ:

country_lookup_example <- tibble(
  country = c("United States", "China", "Japan"),
  short_label = c("US", "China", "Japan")
)

gpfg_latest |>
  distinct(country) |>
  anti_join(country_lookup_example, by = "country") |>
  slice_head(n = 10)


  



anti_join() answers “which keys on the left have no match on the right?” A missing match is not automatically safe to drop. It may reveal a spelling difference, a changed country name, a different definition, or genuinely missing reference data.
Use these checks around a consequential join:

left_only  <- anti_join(left_table, right_table, by = "key")
right_only <- anti_join(right_table, left_table, by = "key")

joined <- left_table |>
  left_join(right_table, by = "key", relationship = "many-to-one")

stopifnot(nrow(joined) == nrow(left_table))
crumbs: 7  Combine Years, Join Tables, and Reshape Data

title: 7  Combine Years, Join Tables, and Reshape Data
text:
7.6 Summarise before comparing years
Company names are not stable identifiers across a decade. For the main trend analysis, aggregate to a defensible grain such as country-year:

country_year <- gpfg_panel |>
  summarise(
    market_value_nok = sum(market_value_nok),
    holding_records = n(),
    .by = c(year, country)
  )

country_year


  



One row now represents one country in one year.
crumbs: 7  Combine Years, Join Tables, and Reshape Data

title: 7  Combine Years, Join Tables, and Reshape Data
crumbs: 7  Combine Years, Join Tables, and Reshape Data

title: 7  Combine Years, Join Tables, and Reshape Data
text:
7.8 What a join cannot solve
A join matches labels; it does not prove that the matched records represent the same real-world entity. Over ten years, company names can change because of mergers, demergers, punctuation, rebranding, or data-entry conventions. Only 3,285 published names appear in all ten teaching snapshots.
For beginner analysis, use country-, region-, or carefully defined industry-level trends. Treat company-level longitudinal matching as an advanced record-linkage project requiring external identifiers and manual verification.

8.2 Newsroom questions
We will investigate four related questions about the latest-year snapshot:

How unequal is the distribution of holding values?
Which countries and industries account for the largest shares?
Which individual holdings are largest?
Does a large market value necessarily mean a large ownership stake?


library(tidyverse)
library(scales)

  "data/processed/gpfg_equities_latest.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

The grain remains one reported equity holding at the latest year-end.

title: 8  Find Patterns in a Single Snapshot
text:
8.3 Describe the distribution
Start with totals and robust summaries:

holding_summary <- gpfg |>
  summarise(
    holding_records = n(),
    total_value_nok = sum(market_value_nok),
    mean_value_nok = mean(market_value_nok),
    median_value_nok = median(market_value_nok),
    p90_value_nok = quantile(market_value_nok, 0.90),
    maximum_value_nok = max(market_value_nok)
  )

holding_summary


  



In a highly skewed distribution, the mean is pulled upward by a small number of very large holdings. Report the median and at least one upper percentile rather than presenting the mean as “typical.”

gpfg |>
  summarise(
    p25 = quantile(market_value_nok, 0.25),
    p50 = quantile(market_value_nok, 0.50),
    p75 = quantile(market_value_nok, 0.75),
    p90 = quantile(market_value_nok, 0.90),
    p99 = quantile(market_value_nok, 0.99)
  )


  



Quantiles answer a precise question: the 90th percentile is the value at or below which 90% of holding records fall. It is not the value of the “average company.”

text:
10.2 Explore before explaining
Exploratory charts help the reporter ask better questions. They can be dense, plain, and numerous. Publication charts are selective and designed around one clear takeaway. Do not decorate the first plot and call it a story.

library(tidyverse)
library(scales)

gpfg <- read_csv(
  "data/processed/gpfg_equities_latest.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

latest_year <- unique(gpfg$year)

title: 10  Exploratory Visualization
10  Exploratory Visualization
text:
10.4 Inspect a skewed distribution
A log scale makes ratios visible across orders of magnitude:

ggplot(gpfg, aes(x = market_value_usd)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 45, fill = "#2C7FB8", color = "white") +
  scale_x_log10(labels = label_dollar(scale_cut = cut_short_scale())) +
  labs(
    title = "Reported holding values span several orders of magnitude",
    subtitle = paste0("Each bar counts equity-holding records in the ", latest_year, " snapshot"),
    x = "Market value in US dollars (log scale)",
    y = "Holding records",
    caption = "Source: Norges Bank Investment Management"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()








The log transformation changes the spacing, not the underlying data. State it in the axis label because many readers interpret horizontal distance as an ordinary additive difference.






Zero and negative values



A log scale cannot display zero or negative values. The latest-year teaching file has positive market values, but the full historical archive contains negative records in 2005–2008. Always check the range before adding a log scale.

title: 10  Exploratory Visualization
10  Exploratory Visualization
text:
10.6 Explore a relationship

ggplot(
  gpfg,
  aes(x = market_value_usd, y = ownership_pct, color = region)
) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.45, size = 1.3) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = label_dollar(scale_cut = cut_short_scale())) +
  labs(
    title = "Large holdings do not always represent large ownership stakes",
    x = "Market value in US dollars (log scale)",
    y = "Ownership (%)",
    color = "Region",
    caption = "Source: Norges Bank Investment Management"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")








The point cloud helps locate exceptions: high ownership with modest market value, or very high market value with a relatively small stake. Those points are reporting leads. Look them up before labelling them.

text:
10.8 An exploratory chart audit
After every chart, ask:

Does the chart’s grain match the question?
Are zeros, missing values, or negative values omitted?
Is the axis transformed or truncated?
Does color encode a variable or merely decorate?
Would a table communicate the exact values more clearly?
Which point, bar, or pattern needs reporting outside the dataset?

10.9 Independent task

a distribution;

title: 11  Explanatory Visualization
text:
11.3 Build a ranked bar chart

country_chart <- top_10_countries |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = market_value_usd,
      y = fct_reorder(country, market_value_usd)
    )
  ) +
  geom_col(fill = "#1769AA", width = 0.72) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = percent(share_of_total, accuracy = 0.1)),
    hjust = -0.15,
    size = 3.4
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    labels = label_dollar(scale = 1e-9, suffix = "B"),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.16))
  ) +
  labs(
    title = paste0(
      top_country$country,
      " accounted for ",
      percent(top_country$share_of_total, accuracy = 0.1),
      " of reported equity value"
    ),
    subtitle = paste0("Ten largest investment markets in NBIM's ", latest_year, " year-end equity holdings"),
    x = "Market value in US dollars",
    y = NULL,
    caption = paste(
      "Labels show share of the full reported equity total.",
      "Source: Norges Bank Investment Management."
    )
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.caption = element_text(hjust = 0)
  )

country_chart








The bars show exact market-value comparisons; the labels answer the denominator question. A rainbow palette would add categories that do not exist, so one color is enough.

section: 11.4 Turn a trend into a clear line chart
text:
11.4 Turn a trend into a clear line chart

gpfg_panel <- readRDS(
  "data/processed/gpfg_equities_last_10_years.rds"
)

annual <- gpfg_panel |>
  summarise(
    market_value_nok = sum(market_value_nok),
    .by = year
  ) |>
  arrange(year) |>
  mutate(market_value_nok_trillions = market_value_nok / 1e12)

panel_years <- annual$year
start_year <- min(panel_years)
end_year <- max(panel_years)

endpoints <- annual |>
  filter(year %in% range(year))


trend_chart <- ggplot(
  annual,
  aes(x = year, y = market_value_nok_trillions)
) +
  geom_line(color = "#1769AA", linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_point(color = "#1769AA", size = 2) +
  geom_text(
    data = endpoints,
    aes(label = paste0(round(market_value_nok_trillions, 1), " tn")),
    vjust = -0.8,
    fontface = "bold"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = panel_years) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = label_number(suffix = " tn"),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.12))
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Reported equity market value more than tripled over the decade",
    subtitle = paste0("Year-end holdings in nominal Norwegian kroner, ", start_year, "–", end_year),
    x = NULL,
    y = "NOK trillions",
    caption = str_wrap(
      paste(
        "Values reflect prices, currencies, purchases, and sales; they are not investment returns.",
        "Source: Norges Bank Investment Management."
      ),
      width = 110
    )
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.title.position = "plot",
    plot.caption = element_text(hjust = 0, size = 8.5),
    plot.caption.position = "plot"
  )

trend_chart








The title is descriptive rather than causal. The subtitle states the time, snapshot basis, currency, and nominal units. The caption names the main interpretive limitation.

title: 11  Explanatory Visualization
section: 11.5 Use color and annotation with restraint
text:
11.5 Use color and annotation with restraint
Color should do a job:

highlight one comparison;
distinguish a small number of series;
encode a meaningful ordered scale; or
signal a consistent category across several charts.

Avoid relying on red versus green alone, which is difficult for many readers. Check that the chart remains understandable in grayscale and that labels carry essential information.
Annotations should explain evidence, not repeat the axis. A useful annotation may identify a documented policy change, classification break, or verified event. Do not annotate a data jump with a causal explanation that the dataset cannot establish.

title: 11  Explanatory Visualization
text:
11.6 Export with reproducible dimensions

ggsave(
  file.path("outputs", paste0("country-holdings-", latest_year, ".png")),
  country_chart,
  width = 8,
  height = 5,
  dpi = 300
)

Choose dimensions for the publishing context. Always inspect the exported file at its intended display size; labels that look fine in RStudio may be unreadable on a phone.

12.3 Get boundary data

world <- ne_countries(
  scale = "medium",
  returnclass = "sf"
)

class(world)

[1] "sf"         "data.frame"


An sf object contains ordinary variables plus a geometry column. Loading sf explicitly ensures that spatial methods are available during a fresh Quarto render.

title: 12  Map Geographic Patterns Carefully
12  Map Geographic Patterns Carefully
text:
12.5 Preserve all polygons
Use the map as the left table so countries without a reported holding remain visible:

world_holdings <- world |>
  filter(name_long != "Antarctica") |>
  left_join(
    country_summary,
    by = c("name_long" = "map_name"),
    relationship = "one-to-one"
  )

stopifnot(!any(st_is_empty(world_holdings)))
stopifnot(
  sum(!is.na(world_holdings$market_value_usd)) == nrow(country_summary)
)

An inner join would silently remove all countries without a match and could make the world appear smaller.

title: 12  Map Geographic Patterns Carefully
text:
12.6 Draw the map

ggplot(world_holdings) +
  geom_sf(
    aes(fill = market_value_usd),
    color = "white",
    linewidth = 0.08
  ) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(
    option = "C",
    trans = "sqrt",
    breaks = c(10e9, 100e9, 500e9),
    labels = label_dollar(scale = 1e-9, suffix = "B"),
    na.value = "#E5E7EB"
  ) +
  coord_sf(expand = FALSE) +
  labs(
    title = "NBIM's reported equity value was concentrated in a limited set of markets",
    subtitle = paste0("Year-end market value by investment market, ", latest_year, "; square-root color scale"),
    fill = "Market value\n(USD)",
    caption = str_wrap(
      paste(
        "Gray indicates no matched holding in the source, not necessarily zero economic exposure.",
        "Sources: Norges Bank Investment Management and Natural Earth."
      ),
      width = 105
    )
  ) +
  guides(

13.7 A methods note readers can understand

We downloaded NBIM’s official year-end listed-equity holdings for 2016–2025 and analyzed the standardized files in R. Each row represents one reported holding at one year-end. We summed nominal market values in Norwegian kroner by investment market and industry and calculated shares using the full annual equity total. Snapshot changes combine prices, currencies, purchases, sales, and changes in portfolio composition; they are not investment flows or returns. We did not match companies longitudinally because published names are not stable identifiers.

14.1 Why this case comes later
The NBIM chapters use a relatively simple holding-level grain. This official Hong Kong dataset is harder: full-time employment is split into many occupation rows, while every other employment status is stored in one row labelled “Not in Full-time Employment.” The row structure is nested and uneven.
That complexity is pedagogically valuable once students can already filter, group, join, and validate. It teaches a central data-journalism lesson: a tidy- looking table can still contain incompatible levels of aggregation.
The source is the Hong Kong Government open-data portal, which describes graduate outcomes for full-time UGC-funded programmes.

15.6 Country codes are not universal
The dataset uses International Olympic Committee codes, while Natural Earth provides ISO-style geographic identifiers. Many codes differ: GER versus DEU, SUI versus CHE, and NED versus NLD. A direct code join would drop many countries.
Use published country names with an explicit concordance for the unmatched labels:

country_medallists <- country_medallists |>
  mutate(
    map_name = recode(
      country,
      "Great Britain" = "United Kingdom",
      "Korea" = "Republic of Korea",
      "Hong Kong, China" = "Hong Kong",
      "Republic of Moldova" = "Moldova",
      "Chinese Taipei" = "Taiwan",
      "Cabo Verde" = "Republic of Cabo Verde",
      "DPR Korea" = "Dem. Rep. Korea",
      "IR Iran" = "Iran",
      "Türkiye" = "Turkey",
      "Czechia" = "Czech Republic"
    )
  ) |>
  filter(!country %in% c("AIN", "EOR"))

AIN represents Individual Neutral Athletes and EOR represents the Refugee Olympic Team. Assigning either delegation to one country polygon would be a substantive error, so they remain in the table but are excluded from the map.

world <- ne_countries(scale = "medium", returnclass = "sf")

unmatched <- country_medallists |>
  anti_join(
    world |>
      st_drop_geometry() |>
      distinct(name_long),
    by = c("map_name" = "name_long")
  )

unmatched


  



The result should have no rows before the spatial join.

world_medallists <- world |>
  filter(name_long != "Antarctica") |>
  left_join(
    country_medallists,
    by = c("name_long" = "map_name"),
    relationship = "one-to-one"
  )

ggplot(world_medallists) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = unique_medallists), color = "white", linewidth = 0.08) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(na.value = "#E5E7EB") +
  labs(
    title = "Unique Paris 2024 medallists by represented country",

    caption = paste(
      "AIN and EOR are not assigned to country polygons.",
      "This is not an official medal-count map."

Grain and limitation
One row represents an already aggregated average salary for one academic year, level of study, and broad programme category. The file does not contain individual graduates or the number of graduates behind each average.
Therefore, this is not a defensible overall annual mean:

salary |>
  summarise(mean_of_means = mean(average_salary_hkd_thousands), .by = year_start)

The code gives every programme-level cell equal weight, even if the underlying numbers of graduates differ greatly. Without counts, a weighted overall average cannot be reconstructed.

no duplicated analytical keys;
same units in every year;
same programme labels at both comparison endpoints; and
explicit treatment of missing programme-years.

)

  filter(country %in% selected_places)



Tasks

Confirm that each selected country-year is unique.
Count missing years by country before filtering them out.
Compare 2000 and 2022 using absolute change in years.
Create a line chart with a common y-axis.
Find the largest one-year rise or fall and verify it against the World Bank source before describing it as a real event.
Explain why pooling all country-years into one correlation or regression would confuse differences between countries with changes within countries.



Required checks

no aggregate areas in the selected comparison;
no duplicate country-years;
the same indicator code across all rows;
missingness reported by country and year; and
endpoint values checked against the publisher.

Appendix A — Publish a Quarto Website
text:
A.1 What Quarto does
Quarto combines Markdown, executable code, citations, and outputs into a website or report. A publishable data project should render from a fresh R session without relying on objects left in the Console.
Current RStudio releases include Quarto. To verify the command-line tool, run this in the Terminal, not the R Console:
The R package named quarto is optional; it is not required to render a Quarto project from RStudio or the Terminal.

title: Appendix A — Publish a Quarto Website
text: quarto check

title: Appendix A — Publish a Quarto Website
text:
A.2 Create a website project
In RStudio, choose File → New Project → New Directory → Quarto Website. A basic project contains:

_quarto.yml — site-wide configuration;
index.qmd — the home page;
other .qmd pages;
optional styles.css; and
an .Rproj file.

Use folders such as:
project/
├── _quarto.yml
├── index.qmd
├── methods.qmd
├── analysis.qmd
├── data/
│   ├── raw/
│   └── processed/
├── scripts/
├── images/
└── outputs/

title: Appendix A — Publish a Quarto Website
text:
A.3 Configure navigation correctly
For a Quarto website, navigation belongs under website: navbar::
project:
  type: website

website:
  title: "My Data Story"
  navbar:
    left:
      - text: Home
        href: index.qmd
      - text: Methods
        href: methods.qmd
      - text: Analysis
        href: analysis.qmd

format:
  html:
    theme: cosmo
    toc: true
Use .qmd targets in the configuration. Quarto creates the corresponding HTML files during rendering.

title: Appendix A — Publish a Quarto Website
text:
A.4 Make every page reproducible
Each page should load the packages and data it needs. Do not assume another page runs first.

library(tidyverse)

analysis_data <- readRDS("data/processed/analysis_data.rds")

Test with:

Session → Restart R;
delete any temporary objects from the Environment;
run quarto render from the project root; and
inspect the rendered site and Terminal output.

title: Appendix A — Publish a Quarto Website
text:
A.5 Preview and publish
Preview locally with the RStudio Render button or:
quarto preview
To publish to Quarto Pub, create an account at quartopub.com and run:
quarto publish
Follow the prompts to choose Quarto Pub and authorize the account. Republishing updates the existing site when you select the same destination.
Publishing is not a substitute for archiving. Preserve the source data, code, and a dated methods note in a repository or institutional storage location.

title: Appendix A — Publish a Quarto Website
text:
A.6 Include files readers need
Quarto automatically includes figures generated by a page, but downloadable data or standalone assets may need to be declared:
project:
  type: website
  resources:
    - data/processed/*.csv
    - downloads/*
Do not publish sensitive data, credentials, embargoed material, or files you do not have permission to redistribute.

title: Appendix A — Publish a Quarto Website
Appendix A — Publish a Quarto Website
text:
A.8 Removing a published site
Deleting the local folder does not remove a published copy. Use the provider’s site dashboard to delete it. Confirm the exact target before deletion; a published URL may already be cited or shared.

title: Appendix B — Final Project Workflow
text:
B.1 Separate preparation from presentation
Use one reproducible script to clean and validate the data, then save a single named object as RDS:
analysis_data <- raw_data |>
  # cleaning steps
  identity()

stopifnot(!anyNA(analysis_data$key))
saveRDS(analysis_data, "data/processed/analysis_data.rds")
Load it explicitly in each page that needs it:
analysis_data <- readRDS("data/processed/analysis_data.rds")
RDS is preferable here to .RData because readRDS() returns one object whose name you choose. load() can silently add several pre-named objects to the environment.

title: Appendix B — Final Project Workflow
text:
B.2 Save a static chart

ggsave(
  "outputs/main-chart.png",
  plot = main_chart,
  width = 8,
  height = 5,
  dpi = 300
)

Insert it with alt text:
![A concise description of the chart's main pattern.](outputs/main-chart.png)

title: Appendix B — Final Project Workflow
section: B.3 Choose geometry from the data structure
text:
B.3 Choose geometry from the data structure
Use a line only when the x variable has a meaningful order, usually time. For a relationship between two unordered numeric variables, use points:

library(ggplot2)

ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = hp, y = qsec)) +
  geom_point(color = "#1769AA") +
  labs(
    title = "Quarter-mile time and horsepower",
    x = "Horsepower",
    y = "Quarter-mile time (seconds)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()








Connecting cars with a line would imply a sequence that does not exist.
